Loss-of-function mutations in BTD lead to impaired recycling of biotin from holocarboxylases, reducing the availability of free biotin for other biotin-dependent carboxylases. Similarly, loss-of-function mutations in MCCC1 directly impair the activity of 3-methylcrotonyl-CoA carboxylase, a key enzyme in the catabolism of leucine and ketogenesis. Both defects converge on the disruption of propionate metabolism and the function of biotin-dependent carboxylases, leading to overlapping clinical features like developmental delay, hypotonia, and seizures.

**How to falsify it:** The absence of biochemical evidence for biotin deficiency or accumulation of 3-methylcrotonyl-CoA and its metabolites in patients with mutations in BTD or MCCC1, respectively, would falsify this hypothesis. Furthermore, the identification of pathogenic variants in BTD or MCCC1 with frequencies exceeding 1% in gnomAD would cast doubt on their causal role. _(variant: null)_

**Why it matters:** Understanding this mechanistic link can inform targeted metabolic screening and management strategies for patients presenting with overlapping symptoms. Early diagnosis and intervention, including biotin supplementation in BTD and dietary management in MCCC1 deficiency, are crucial for improving neurological outcomes.
